title: Capitalism and Its Moral Basis
summary: Laissez-faire capitalism as the system that follows from rights, not as a brute economic preference.

lessons.title: Name the system
lessons.objective: Identify laissez-faire capitalism as the political system this unit defends.

exercises.prompt: Which political system does this unit defend?

choices.text: Laissez-faire capitalism
A mixed economy that steers trade
Socialism with private shops allowed
Rule by whoever is richest

feedback.note: The system named here is laissez-faire capitalism, the political order that leaves production and trade free.

exercises.prompt: Match each label to what it names in this unit.

feedback.note: Capitalism is the system. Laissez-faire says how free it is. The moral basis is the reason, not a separate hobby.

exercises.prompt: Name the system in full.

feedback.note: The full name matters. Capitalism here means laissez-faire capitalism, not a steered or favored economy.

exercises.prompt: In the one-foot list of branches, what stands beside Politics?

choices.text: Capitalism
Reason
Self-interest
Objective Reality

feedback.note: Politics is the branch, and capitalism is the answer this philosophy gives for that branch.

exercises.prompt: Build the claim this lesson is teaching.

feedback.note: The political conclusion is laissez-faire capitalism. The extra tokens name the opposite move.

exercises.prompt: What kind of claim is the defense of this system?

choices.text: A political conclusion
A rule about painting
A tip about shopping
A mood about money

feedback.note: Capitalism belongs on the politics floor. It is the social system, not a shopping hint or an art style.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to the system it points to.

pairs.left: The name of the politics branch’s answer

feedback.note: Free production and trade is the system. Steering production is what this unit is not defending.

exercises.prompt: Finish the branch line in plain words.

feedback.note: On the one-foot list, the politics line is Capitalism. The other words belong to other branches.

exercises.prompt: Which wording is too vague for this unit’s answer?

choices.text: Whatever helps business this year
Laissez-faire capitalism
A system of free production and trade
The political system that follows in this philosophy

feedback.note: A yearly business tactic is not the system. The name to hold is laissez-faire capitalism.

exercises.prompt: Put the short name in order.

feedback.note: Laissez-faire capitalism is the system this unit names. It is not filed as a whim.

lessons.title: It follows from rights
lessons.objective: Explain that the case for laissez-faire capitalism starts from individual rights.

exercises.prompt: What does laissez-faire capitalism follow from, on this account?

choices.text: Individual rights
A poll about favorite shops
Last year’s growth number alone
An old custom with no reason

feedback.note: The system follows from rights. A poll, a growth figure, or a bare custom is not the basis.

exercises.prompt: Complete the unit’s central claim.

parts.text: , not from a brute economic preference.

feedback.note: Rights are the starting point. A brute preference for one kind of economy is what the claim refuses.

exercises.prompt: Match each starting point to the conclusion it supports here.

pairs.right: A system that leaves that action free
The moral case for the system drops with them

feedback.note: The political system is the social form of the rights. Without the rights, this unit’s reason for capitalism is gone.

exercises.prompt: Why is capitalism called a moral conclusion here?

choices.text: It is what respecting rights requires
It makes a few people richer by design
It is older than other systems
It is easier to diagram

feedback.note: The moral basis is rights. Age, a diagram, or a plan to enrich a few is not that basis.

exercises.prompt: Build the order this lesson uses.

feedback.note: Rights come first. Laissez-faire capitalism is the system that follows, not a coin flip.

exercises.prompt: If someone keeps the rights and drops free trade, what has gone wrong on this account?

choices.text: The system no longer matches the rights
Nothing, rights ignore action
Only the arithmetic is off
Only the style of shops changed

feedback.note: Rights sanction freedom of action, including production and trade. A system that cancels that freedom has left the rights behind.

exercises.prompt: Fill both blanks.

feedback.note: Keep the two words apart: rights are the basis, and capitalism is the system that follows.

exercises.prompt: Match the question to the answer this unit gives.

feedback.note: The why is rights. The what is laissez-faire capitalism. A brute economic preference is the answer this unit rejects.

exercises.prompt: A right, in the sense this unit relies on, sanctions what?

choices.text: Freedom of action in a social setting
A gift of goods from others
A turn to run other people’s work
A feeling that one should win

feedback.note: Rights here sanction freedom of action among other people. They are not a claim on someone else’s goods or a mood.

exercises.prompt: State the dependence in one line.

feedback.note: Take away rights and this unit’s moral basis for laissez-faire capitalism is gone.

lessons.title: Not a brute preference
lessons.objective: Reject the idea that capitalism is only a taste for markets or a growth trick.

exercises.prompt: Which defense does this unit refuse?

choices.text: Capitalism as a brute economic preference
Capitalism as what follows from rights
Capitalism as laissez-faire
Capitalism as a moral conclusion

feedback.note: A brute economic preference is the defense this unit sets aside. The defense it keeps is rights.

exercises.prompt: Match each slogan to how this unit treats it.

pairs.left: It grew the numbers, so it is right
Rights require freedom to produce and trade

feedback.note: Liking markets, or pointing only at results, is not the case. The case is that rights require the freedom.

exercises.prompt: Finish the contrast.

parts.text: The system is not a brute

feedback.note: The phrase to reject is brute economic preference. Moral, political, and legal are the kind of claim the unit is making instead.

exercises.prompt: Someone says capitalism is useful but morally blank. What does this unit say?

choices.text: The case is moral: it follows from rights
Yes, usefulness is the whole case
Politics has no moral basis at all
Any system is moral if output rises

feedback.note: Usefulness is not the substitute for a moral basis. This unit treats laissez-faire capitalism as what rights require.

exercises.prompt: Build the refusal.

feedback.note: A preference is not a foundation. The system is not parked on taste.

exercises.prompt: Which pair confuses a result with a basis?

choices.text: Growth happened, therefore the system is justified
Rights hold, therefore free trade follows
The name is laissez-faire capitalism
A brute preference is not enough

feedback.note: A result can be welcome and still not be the reason. The reason in this unit is rights, not the fact that output moved.

exercises.prompt: Sort each item as basis or not.

pairs.left: A demand that the numbers look good first

feedback.note: Only rights are the basis in this unit. Taste and a demand for pretty numbers are the items being set aside.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two roles.

feedback.note: Preference is refused as the basis. Rights are accepted as the basis.

exercises.prompt: If two people prefer different economies, what does this unit still claim?

choices.text: The rights still pick out laissez-faire capitalism
Both preferences are equally the system
No system can be named
The louder preference wins

feedback.note: Preferences can clash. The unit does not settle the clash by volume. It points back to rights.

exercises.prompt: State what the unit puts in place of a preference.

feedback.note: Where a brute preference would have stood, this unit puts rights.

lessons.title: What laissez-faire rules out
lessons.objective: State what laissez-faire rules out: running the economy and handing out special favors.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, laissez-faire means officials do what?

choices.text: Leave production and trade alone
Pick the winning firms
Set each person’s work
Divide the product by a plan

feedback.note: Laissez-faire means hands off production and trade. Picking winners, assigning work, or dividing the product is the opposite.

exercises.prompt: Match each practice to the verdict.

pairs.left: A special favor for one firm
A plan that runs the whole economy
Trade by the parties’ own choice

feedback.note: Favors and a run economy are what laissez-faire rules out. Trade by the parties’ own choice is what it leaves in place.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule of thumb.

feedback.note: Special favors are ruled out, and so is an economy run from above. Rights and trade are not the things being banned.

exercises.prompt: Why is a special favor not a small exception here?

choices.text: It still uses politics to steer trade
It is too small to count as politics
Kindness always overrides rights
Firms have a right to be favored

feedback.note: A favor is still a decision to steer who gains in trade. Laissez-faire does not keep a side door for that.

exercises.prompt: Build what the system leaves free.

feedback.note: Production and trade stay with the people who choose them. Assignment from above is the distractor.

exercises.prompt: Which arrangement still counts as laissez-faire?

choices.text: Two people trade because both agree
An office assigns each town a quota
A friend of the ruler gets the only license
A board sets every price for a goal

feedback.note: Agreement between the parties is the free trade this system protects. Quotas, exclusive licenses, and dictated prices are steering.

exercises.prompt: Match the short name to the ban.

feedback.note: Laissez-faire is the refusal of both a privilege for the connected and official direction of production.

exercises.prompt: Fill the contrast.

feedback.note: Consent of the parties is the method. Favor is the method laissez-faire rules out.

exercises.prompt: Hands off the economy is required here because of what?

choices.text: Rights to act, including to produce and trade
Officials dislike paperwork
A fashion for small offices
Markets always feel pleasant

feedback.note: The hands-off rule is not a mood about offices. It is what leaving people’s rights intact requires.

lessons.title: One chain
lessons.objective: Hold one order: each person is an end, rights follow, and laissez-faire capitalism is the system that respects those rights.

exercises.prompt: Which order matches this unit?

choices.text: Each person is an end, then rights, then laissez-faire capitalism
Pick an economy first, then invent rights to fit it
Check growth first, then decide if persons matter
Mix every system so nobody’s principle wins

feedback.note: The chain runs from the person as an end, to rights, to the system. It does not start from a preferred chart.

exercises.prompt: Build that order.

feedback.note: Start from the person as an end. Rights come next. Laissez-faire capitalism is the political system at the end of that chain.

exercises.prompt: Match each step to its job in the chain.

pairs.left: Man is an end in himself

pairs.right: The principle for action among people

feedback.note: Three jobs, one chain: a moral start, a principle for social action, and the political system that respects it.

exercises.prompt: What does it mean here to treat a person as an end?

choices.text: He lives for his own life, not as a tool of others
He is available for anyone’s project
The group may spend him if it votes
He has no standing in politics

feedback.note: An end in himself is not a resource for other people’s plans. That is the moral start this political system rests on.

exercises.prompt: Fill the chain.

feedback.note: After the person as an end come rights, and after rights comes capitalism. A whim or a quota is not a step in the chain.

exercises.prompt: Reversing the chain would mean what?

choices.text: Choosing an economy first and bending rights to fit
The same argument in a shorter sentence
A stricter respect for rights
Dropping politics entirely

feedback.note: Starting from a preferred economy and trimming rights to match is the reverse of this unit. The rights come first.

exercises.prompt: Match the break to the step it drops.

pairs.left: People may be used as tools

feedback.note: Each break knocks out one step. Using people as tools, making freedom optional, or steering trade by favor each leaves the chain.

exercises.prompt: State the whole unit in one line.

feedback.note: The line to keep is that capitalism follows from rights. Taste is the rival the unit will not use.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is the unit’s summary, in plain words?

choices.text: Laissez-faire capitalism follows from rights, not from a brute economic preference
Buy from the largest store
Use any mix of controls that raises output
Politics should avoid naming a system

feedback.note: That one sentence is the unit: the system follows from rights, and a brute economic preference is not a stand-in.

exercises.prompt: Close the unit.

parts.text: Laissez-faire capitalism is the system that

feedback.note: The last line is the title’s point: the system follows from rights. It does not ignore them, and it is not taken from a poll.
